overview: Macquarie Group is a global diversified financial services group founded in Australia in 1969, operating in 30 markets across asset management, retail and business banking, wealth management, and advisory, risk and capital solutions spanning debt, equity, financial markets and commodities. It is regulated by APRA as a Non-Operating Holding Company of Macquarie Bank Limited, an authorised deposit-taking institution, and reported 57 consecutive years of unbroken annual profitability through FY2026 (year ended 31 March 2026). The group is organised into four operating segments -- Macquarie Asset Management (MAM), Banking and Financial Services (BFS), Commodities and Global Markets (CGM) and Macquarie Capital -- with the majority of income (>80% for MAM, CGM and Macquarie Capital) generated outside Australia.

business_model.summary: Macquarie earns fee, commission, net interest, trading and investment income across four distinct segments: a global infrastructure/real-asset/private-credit fund manager earning base and performance fees (MAM); a domestic Australian retail/business bank and wealth platform earning net interest margin and platform fees (BFS); a global commodities and financial markets trading, financing and risk-management business earning trading, risk-management and net interest income (CGM); and an advisory, capital markets, principal investing and private credit business earning fees, brokerage and investment gains (Macquarie Capital). FY2026 net operating income of $A19,477m grew 13% YoY and net profit of $A4,847m grew 30% YoY, with earnings growth across all four segments; ROE rose to 14% from ~11% in the prior two years.

revenue_streams.name: Commodities and Global Markets (CGM) - net profit contribution
Macquarie Asset Management (MAM) - net profit contribution
Banking and Financial Services (BFS) - net profit contribution

business_model.customer_type: Mixed: institutional, corporate, government and wholesale clients (MAM, CGM, Macquarie Capital) plus ~2.3 million Australian retail/business banking and wealth customers (BFS)
business_model.geographic_mix: ANZ ~50% of staff/home market for BFS; MAM generates 87% of income outside Australia, CGM 82% outside Australia, Macquarie Capital 84% outside Australia; global operations across EMEA (~15% of staff), Americas (~12%), Asia (~23%)

main_competitors: Big Four Australian banks (CBA, Westpac, NAB, ANZ) in domestic banking
competitive_position.market_position: World's largest manager of infrastructure assets via MAM (over $A722.1 billion in assets globally, $A325.9 billion in Australia, trusted by nine of the top ten Australian superannuation funds); leading Australian M&A adviser by volume and value; one of Australia's fastest-growing digital banks (>6% share of deposits, >7% share of home loans); a top-tier global commodities trading and risk-management franchise

moat_factors.description: 50+ years of pioneering infrastructure asset management (first toll road listing, Sydney Airport privatisation, motor vehicle registry commercialisation) gives MAM deep origination networks and fund-investor trust ($722bn AUM globally)
Annuity-style businesses (MAM base fees, BFS) balance markets-facing businesses (CGM, Macquarie Capital), smoothing earnings and enabling 57 consecutive profitable years
Deep expertise in physical and financial gas/power/oil markets and structured financing provides differentiated, hard-to-replicate income streams (CGM is now the largest profit contributor)
Willingness to invest alongside clients and align staff/shareholder interests supports long-term relationships and deal flow
APRA-regulated NOHC/ADI status is a barrier to entry, though it also invites intensive supervision

weaknesses: Repeated regulatory and compliance failures (APRA overlays, ASIC litigation) that have required years of remediation and damaged reputation
Earnings volatility from performance fees, investment/asset-realisation gains and trading income makes results less predictable than pure annuity businesses
Domestic banking business is a relatively small player against Australia's Big Four incumbents
Heavy foreign-currency income exposure creates AUD translation risk to reported earnings

growth_drivers: Continued expansion of MAM's global infrastructure, real estate and private credit platforms (record Macquarie Infrastructure Partners VI fund close; Macquarie Green Energy Transition Solutions fund; entry into new asset classes like data centres)
AI-driven demand for data centre and energy infrastructure financing and investment (Aligned Data Centers, Sandow Lake Energy Station, digital infrastructure financing)
Growth of BFS digital banking platform and market share gains in Australian home loans, deposits and wealth management
CGM's expansion into new geographies and adjacent commodities (LNG, Flexible Power Platform, Erova Energy acquisition) capturing energy-transition volatility and financing demand
Macquarie Capital advisory and private credit growth, including participation in sovereign-resilience/critical-minerals/defence-related M&A and financing
Large completed/announced M&A such as the ~$A11.7bn MAM-led consortium acquisition of Qube Holdings (completed August 2026), adding infrastructure-like logistics assets under management
Capital redeployment as management seeks attractive risk-adjusted return opportunities following conclusion of the on-market share buyback

business.risk: Earnings concentration in performance fees and gains on sale
business.description: FY2026 growth was significantly aided by one-off gains (OnStream meters divestment, North American/European public investments sale, equity investment exits); underlying run-rate earnings power is less than headline growth suggests
Management specifically cited lower margins from lending and deposit competition partially offsetting BFS volume growth
Rapid AI adoption could reshape how financial services are delivered, competed for and regulated, intensifying competitive and cyber pressures

financial.description: A significant proportion of net income is denominated in foreign currency; AUD appreciation reduces reported AUD earnings (FY2026 equity fell $A1.7bn from FX translation reserve movements)
Reliance on deposits and wholesale debt markets exposes Macquarie to higher funding costs or reduced market access in stress scenarios
Credit and other impairment charges rose 96% YoY in FY2026 due to portfolio growth, macro uncertainty and specific counterparty impairments

regulatory.description: A $A500m operational risk capital overlay remains in place and unchanged; liquidity (NCO) add-ons were only partially reduced (25%→15% from Feb 2026) and remain until all remediation is confirmed complete

ASIC brought court action (settled March 2026) over transaction-reporting failures; separately, the Federal Court found Macquarie Investment Management contravened the Corporations Act over the Shield Master Fund, with ~$A321m paid to affected members and related proceedings against other trustees continuing; further class actions possible
A significant minority 'strike' against the FY2025 Remuneration Report reflects investor concern about how regulatory/compliance shortcomings are reflected in executive pay

regulatory.risk: M&A/antitrust approval risk on large transactions
regulatory.description: The Qube Holdings acquisition and similar large MAM-led deals require FIRB/ACCC and other regulatory approvals that can delay or block completion
Increasing regulatory change at global and Australian levels can affect capital, funding requirements and profitability across all segments

macro.description: Management cites armed-conflict proliferation, energy/commodity supply disruption and elevated public debt burdens as ongoing headwinds to the operating environment

macro.risk: Interest rate and market volatility sensitivity
macro.description: Trading, risk-management and investment income (particularly in CGM and Macquarie Capital) is sensitive to interest rate moves and market volatility, which can cut both ways

CGM's derivative and inventory positions are directly exposed to gas, power and oil price volatility, which drove large swings in trading/investment income and balance sheet derivative assets/liabilities in FY2026

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Diversified global financial services and asset management remains structurally supported by infrastructure investment needs (energy transition, AI/data-centre buildout, sovereign resilience/reshoring), though wholesale markets and M&A activity remain cyclical and sensitive to rates and geopolitics
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high - BFS and MAM base fees are relatively annuity-like, but CGM trading/investment income and Macquarie Capital advisory/principal-investing income are cyclical and can swing significantly with market conditions and deal activity
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - net interest income in BFS benefits from loan/deposit growth but faces margin competition; CGM and Group Treasury funding costs are directly affected by rate levels
key_input_costs: Wholesale funding costs (deposits, senior unsecured debt, securitisation)

recent_developments.event: FY2026 results: net profit of $A4,847m, up 30% YoY (third consecutive year of earnings growth, second-highest result in company history); ROE rose to 14%; earnings grew across all four operating segments, led by CGM (+49%)

Board resolved final dividend of $A4.20/share, taking FY2026 total dividend to $A7.00/share, consistent with 50-70% payout policy; on-market share buyback concluded given business growth and market conditions
Macquarie reached a court-approved settlement with ASIC over transaction-reporting failures dating back several years, following ASIC's May 2025 court action
APRA partially eased Macquarie Bank's liquidity (NCO) add-on from 25% to 15%, citing remediation progress, while keeping the $A500m operational risk capital overlay unchanged

Macquarie Asset Management-led consortium (with UniSuper and Pontegadea) agreed to acquire Qube Holdings for $A5.20/share cash, implying an ~$A11.7bn (US$8.3bn) enterprise value; deal completed 14 August 2026 after shareholder and regulatory approval

Federal Court found Macquarie Investment Management contravened the Corporations Act in relation to the Shield Master Fund; Macquarie paid ~$A321m to affected members to return 100% of net capital invested, with related ASIC proceedings against other trustees (Equity Trustees, Diversa) continuing
2025 AGM: a significant minority of shareholders voted against the Remuneration Report (a 'strike'), citing dissatisfaction with how regulatory/compliance issues were reflected in executive pay

Completed sale of North American and European public investments business (MAM) and divestment of the OnStream smart-meter platform (CGM/Asset Finance), both generating material gains recognised in FY2026 results
CGM acquired 100% of Erova Energy (UK/Ireland renewable route-to-market and optimisation services)

items.notes: Macquarie does not issue formal point or range earnings guidance; management instead provides qualitative outlook commentary and short-term factors to watch
FY2026 total dividend of $A7.00/share consistent with the longstanding payout policy

items.metric: CET1 capital ratio (Bank Group, APRA Basel III)
items.target: Maintain well above 9% minimum (12.8% actual at FY2026 year-end; 17.5% on Harmonised Basel III)
items.notes: Group capital surplus of $A9.3bn; management reiterated a 'cautious' and 'conservative approach to capital, funding and liquidity'

items.target: On-market buyback concluded; no further purchases currently expected
items.notes: Given significant business growth and prevailing market conditions, management is instead prioritising redeployment of capital into opportunities offering attractive risk-adjusted returns

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Glenn Stevens and CEO Shemara Wikramanayake both flagged 'no shortage of challenges' in the operating environment -- armed conflict, energy/supply-chain disruption, high public debt, and AI-driven technological disruption -- but noted all four client franchises grew and underlying (ex one-off) performance improved. Short-term outlook factors cited: global economic conditions, inflation and interest rates, volatility events, geopolitical events, completion of period-end reviews and transactions, geographic income mix/FX, and potential tax or regulatory changes. Management continues to emphasize a conservative, well-capitalised balance sheet and disciplined capital reallocation toward higher-return activities, while regulatory remediation (APRA overlays, post-Shield/ASIC matters) continues but is described as 'proceeding on schedule.'

bull_case: Diversified, largely non-Australian-dollar-denominated global franchise with genuine scale advantages in infrastructure/real-asset fund management (largest in the world) that benefits from structural AI/data-centre and energy-transition capital demand

57 consecutive years of unbroken profitability with a conservative, well-capitalised balance sheet (CET1 12.8% APRA / 17.5% Harmonised Basel III, $A9.3bn capital surplus) provides resilience through cycles

FY2026 delivered 30% profit growth and 14% ROE with earnings growth across all four segments, and large completed transactions (Qube Holdings) demonstrate continued ability to deploy capital at scale into attractive infrastructure assets

Regulatory overhang is gradually easing -- APRA has begun reducing liquidity add-ons and Macquarie reached settlement/resolution on ASIC and Shield Master Fund matters, removing sources of uncertainty
Consensus analyst rating is Buy (average 12-month price target implying high-single-digit upside from current levels around $A240-250), reflecting confidence in the franchise despite regulatory noise
bear_case: A meaningful share of FY2026 earnings growth came from one-off gains on sale (OnStream, public investments divestiture, equity exits) rather than pure run-rate improvement, making the 30% profit growth partly unrepeatable

Regulatory risk remains elevated and expensive: the $A500m APRA operational risk capital overlay is unchanged, liquidity add-ons are only partially removed, and Shield Master Fund/ASIC-related litigation and reputational damage could continue via further class actions and enforcement against related trustees

Trading/investment income-heavy segments (CGM, Macquarie Capital) are inherently more volatile and market-dependent than pure asset-management annuity businesses, and impairment charges rose sharply (+96% YoY) amid macro uncertainty

Heavy foreign-currency income exposure (>80% of MAM, CGM, Macquarie Capital income generated offshore) creates AUD translation risk that can suppress reported earnings independent of underlying business performance
Conclusion of the share buyback and shareholder 'strike' on the Remuneration Report signal capital-return and governance friction that could weigh on investor sentiment near-term
